data.title: Alopecia areata — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Alopecia areata** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Define alopecia areata (AA).**
- Chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated, non-scarring hair loss with well-circumscribed patches of hair loss on scalp or any hair-bearing area, with preserved follicular openings; affects ~2% lifetime; any age, peak 20–40 y

**Q2. Classify alopecias (PYQ).**
- Non-scarring (non-cicatricial): AA, androgenetic alopecia, telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, trichotillomania, traction (early), tinea capitis (non-inflammatory), secondary syphilis, hair shaft defects, hypothyroidism, nutritional
- Scarring (cicatricial) — primary: lymphocytic (DLE, LPP, frontal fibrosing alopecia, central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia, pseudopelade of Brocq), neutrophilic (folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis), mixed (acne keloidalis, erosive pustular dermatosis); secondary: burns, radiation, trauma, kerion, tumours, morphoea, infections (lupus vulgaris)

**Q3. Describe the hair cycle (PYQ).**
- Anagen (growth): 2–7 years, ~85–90% of scalp hairs, determines length
- Catagen (regression): 2–3 weeks, ~1%
- Telogen (rest): ~3 months, 10–15%; club hair shed in exogen
- Kenogen: empty follicle interval; scalp has ~100,000 hairs, normal shedding 50–100/day; growth ~1 cm/month

**Q4. Pathogenesis of AA.**
- Collapse of immune privilege of anagen hair bulb (reduced MHC I, TGF-β, α-MSH) → autoreactive CD8+NKG2D+ T cells attack follicular autoantigens (melanocyte/keratinocyte), IFN-γ and IL-15 via JAK–STAT signalling → follicle forced into dystrophic anagen/telogen; follicle stem cells spared (non-scarring, reversible)
- Genetic (HLA-DQB1, ULBP, CTLA4, IL2RA), family history 10–20%, stress, viral infections, vaccination triggers
- Associations: atopy, thyroid autoimmunity, vitiligo, Down syndrome, APECED, lupus, diabetes, iron deficiency

**Q5. Clinical patterns and signs.**
- Patchy (commonest), ophiasis (band along occipital and temporal margins — poor prognosis), sisaipho (inverse ophiasis — frontoparietal), diffuse (acute diffuse and total alopecia — mimics TE), alopecia totalis (whole scalp), universalis (all body hair), reticular
- Exclamation-mark hairs (tapering proximal ends) at active edge, positive pull test at margin, regrowth with white (vellus) hairs first, sparing of grey hairs ('sudden whitening overnight')
- Nails (10–60%): fine regular geometric pitting, trachyonychia, Beau's lines, red lunulae, onychomadesis

**Q6. Trichoscopy in AA.**
- Yellow dots (keratin in empty follicles), black dots (cadaverised hairs — active), exclamation-mark hairs, broken hairs, tapered hairs, short vellus/regrowing hairs, Pohl–Pinkus constrictions

**Q7. Histopathology.**
- Peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate ('swarm of bees') around anagen bulbs (acute), increased catagen/telogen hairs, miniaturised follicles, fibrous streamers, pigment casts, eosinophils; no scarring

**Q8. Severity assessment.**
- SALT score (Severity of Alopecia Tool): % scalp hair loss — vertex 40%, posterior 24%, each side 18% — S1 <25%, S2 25–49, S3 50–74, S4 75–99, S5 100%; severe AA = SALT ≥50
- Alopecia areata investigator global assessment (AA-IGA)

**Q9. Differential diagnosis.**
- Tinea capitis (scaling, broken hairs, KOH), trichotillomania (bizarre shapes, broken hairs of varying length, no exclamation-mark hairs, trichoscopy — flame hairs, tulip hairs, V-sign), telogen effluvium (diffuse, positive pull test everywhere), secondary syphilis (moth-eaten), androgenetic alopecia (diffuse AA), early scarring alopecia, traction alopecia, loose anagen syndrome, temporal triangular alopecia (congenital)

**Q10. Investigations.**
- Clinical/trichoscopy; thyroid function and antibodies, CBC, ferritin, vitamin D, blood sugar; VDRL if moth-eaten; KOH; biopsy if doubtful

**Q11. Treatment.**
- Limited patchy (<50%): intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 2.5–10 mg/ml (5 mg/ml commonly) every 4–6 weeks (first line in adults), super-potent topical steroids (children), minoxidil 5% adjunct, topical immunotherapy for chronic (DPCP, SADBE — induce allergic contact dermatitis), anthralin short contact (children)
- Extensive/rapidly progressive: oral mini-pulse betamethasone/dexamethasone 5 mg twice weekly, pulse methylprednisolone, short oral prednisolone; methotrexate (± low-dose steroid), azathioprine, cyclosporine, oral minoxidil
- JAK inhibitors for severe AA (SALT ≥50): baricitinib 4 mg (FDA 2022, adults; approved in India), ritlecitinib 50 mg (≥12 y), deuruxolitinib; tofacitinib off-label — monitor CBC, lipids, LFT, infections (TB/HZV screening)
- Supportive: wigs, hair pieces, eyebrow tattooing/microblading, counselling, support groups

**Q12. Prognosis.**
- ~50% of limited patchy AA regrow within a year without treatment; poor prognostic factors — onset in childhood, extensive (totalis/universalis), ophiasis, long duration (>1 y), nail changes, atopy, family history, associated autoimmunity, Down syndrome

## Quick spotter facts
- Smooth round patch with exclamation-mark hairs — AA
- Yellow dots, black dots on trichoscopy
- Severe AA — baricitinib/ritlecitinib

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Alopecia areata); SALT score; JAK inhibitor approvals. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
